title: Not by might (Zechariah 4:6)
hookLine: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit
tomorrow: your king comes on a donkey

cards: Same city, same year, same half-built temple as yesterday. Haggai told the people to build, and they did.

The man in charge is Zerubbabel, the governor, a descendant of the old kings, with a small crew of returned exiles, not much money, hostile neighbors, and a foundation that looks like nothing next to the stories of Solomon's temple.

Haggai himself asks who is left who saw the first house in its glory, and whether this one looks like nothing beside it. Into that discouragement steps a second prophet, Zechariah. He doesn't bring a budget.

teach.h: A GOLDEN LAMPSTAND, TWO OLIVE TREES.
teach.b: Zechariah sees a lampstand of solid gold with seven lamps, and on either side, two olive trees that seem to feed oil straight into the lamps. Nobody presses olives, hauls jars or refills anything.

teach.h: OIL FROM A SOURCE BEYOND THE LAMP.
teach.b: The light just keeps burning, fed from a source the lamps don't control. Zechariah asks the angel what it means.
The answer, in the King James Bible: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts."
The word for might can also mean an army, or wealth, or strength. Power is the strength of your own arm. Zerubbabel has neither, and God says that's fine.
That's not how this gets built. Then a picture for the governor's problem: "Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain."
The mountain might be the opposition, or the sheer size of the task. Either way, it flattens. When the last stone goes on, the people will shout grace, grace unto it.
A few verses later comes a question: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" The little foundation that looked like nothing is not to be despised. Small beginnings count.

teach.h: NOT BY MIGHT, NOR BY POWER, BUT BY MY SPIRIT.
teach.b: Some Christians read the vision as a picture of the Holy Spirit, the oil that keeps the lamp burning.
Others hear a word for any work that seems too big for the people doing it: churches, families, movements, one person trying to change. The work still needs hands; Zerubbabel still lays the stones.
But the light isn't his to manufacture.

how: Some Christians quote Zechariah 4:6 when starting a work that feels too big, such as founding a church or a ministry, and some read the lampstand's oil as a picture of the Holy Spirit.

o: the prophet who saw a golden lampstand
the king who built the first, grand temple
the governor leading the rebuild with a small crew

games.q: what's inside Zechariah 4 — tap the pairs.

s: "not by might" means the temple built itself
Zerubbabel still lays the stones. the point is that the strength behind the work is God's spirit.
Haggai asks whether the new temple looks like nothing beside the old
he asks who is left who saw the first house in its glory (Haggai 2:3).
in the vision, the lamps are filled by hand
two olive trees feed the oil straight into them, from a source the lamps don't control.

games.q: you're Zerubbabel. small crew, little money, hostile neighbors, and a foundation that looks like nothing beside Solomon's. what word does Zechariah bring you?
o: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
wait until you can match Solomon.
games.why: "not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts." and: who hath despised the day of small things?

practice: Think of something you've been pushing on hard, a person you're trying to change, a project that won't move, and notice the clench in your jaw, shoulders or stomach.

For a few breaths, loosen it: not quitting, since Zerubbabel kept building, just admitting the oil isn't yours to make. If you pray, hand that one thing to God's spirit; if not, simply let your hands open on your lap.

wordCard.voice: Zerubbabel. The governor with a small crew and a big job, told the mountain before him would become a plain, not by might but by God's spirit.

orig.note: Hebrew: might. it can also mean an army, wealth or strength: everything Zerubbabel didn't have.

carryVoice: Your line: grace, grace unto it. Small beginnings count, even when they look like nothing. See you tomorrow.
